reply.answer:
For your return, aim for a balanced, predictable bike—not your old race pace straight away. **Start with stock suspension settings and temperature/elevation-correct jetting**, then change one thing at a time.

### Initial jetting
These are Husqvarna’s stock-engine/exhaust settings for **0–300 m (0–984 ft)**, not all Texas locations:

| Temperature | Main jet | Pilot jet | Needle clip | Air screw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16–24°C (61–75°F) | 450 | 35 | 3rd from top | 1.5 turns out |
| 25–36°C (77–97°F) | 440 | 32.5 | 3rd from top | 1.5 turns out |
| 37–49°C (99–120°F) | 430 | 32.5 | 3rd from top | 2 turns out |

All three use the **6BFY42-71 needle**. Check what is actually installed before buying jets; an aftermarket pipe or engine work means these are starting points, not a finished tune. Stop riding if it pings under load—don’t keep testing leaner settings.

### Suspension
For stock suspension, Husqvarna’s baseline is:
- **Fork:** 10.1 bar (146 psi), compression 12 clicks out, rebound 12 clicks out. This is an air fork: pressure replaces a coil-spring rate. Check cold with the front wheel unloaded.
- **Shock:** low-speed compression 15 clicks out, high-speed compression 1.5 turns out, rebound 15 clicks out.
- **Sag:** 105 mm (4.13 in) with you in full gear; 35 mm (1.38 in) with the bike standing without you.

Your saved geared weight is **185 lb**. Husqvarna’s 75–85 kg (165–187 lb) band lists a **shock spring 42 N/mm**; the chart does not specify gear inclusion. Confirm the fitted spring with sag: too little rider-off sag after setting rider sag points to a spring that’s too soft. If it’s revalved, get the tuner’s baseline for your weight instead.

### Chassis and first rides
Husqvarna specifies **1.0 bar (15 psi) cold, front and rear**. Start there with air-filled tires. Leave fork height alone initially, check that the fork moves freely, and inspect steering/linkage bearings before tuning around harshness.

At 6 feet tall, set lever reach and angle so you can stand with relaxed wrists; don’t automatically add tall bar risers. Rebuild braking and standing habits at an easy pace before chasing jumps or old lap times.

**Which Texas town or track will you ride, and what temperatures do you expect?** That will narrow the jetting choice.

I’d **leave the exhaust and ECU stock for now**. After 10 years off, suspension setup and a few coached practice sessions will do more for you than extra horsepower.

1. **Fresh protective gear**, especially if your helmet and boots are from before the break.

Yamaha’s free **Power Tuner app** adjusts the stock ECU—an aftermarket ECU isn’t required. It includes three preloaded engine maps, and the bike holds two selectable maps: **light off = map 1; light on = map 2**.

**Get light on the seat before the chop, not after it starts kicking you.** Sitting heavily through exit bumps sends every hit into you and makes it harder to stay smooth.

- **While it’s still turning:** keep pressure through the outside peg, your body more upright than the bike, and your elbows bent. Hover just above the seat where the line allows—don’t stand tall or hang off the back.
- **As the turn opens:** bring your inside foot back onto the peg and rise into a low standing position, knees soft. Hold yourself with your legs, not a death grip on the bars.
- **Feed the power in:** build throttle smoothly rather than snapping it open. Look beyond the chop and try a smoother exit line, even if it’s slightly longer.

Next practice, ride that exit **three times at a comfortable pace**, focusing only on getting light on the seat before the first bump. Don’t force extra speed yet.

**Your KX isn’t suddenly slow because it’s a 2013.** A healthy older 450 still has substantial power; engine condition matters more than age alone. I can’t confirm the exact performance gap to a current YZ450F without comparable measurements. Newer does not automatically mean easier to ride.

**A 350 is easier to manage, not necessarily easier to ride your way.** General guidance:
- **350:** Less torque to manage, usually less tiring under acceleration and easier to change direction. But matching a 450’s drive generally means more rpm, shifting and clutch use—especially with your 200 lb aboard. It won’t necessarily be dramatically lighter on a scale.
- **450:** Easier to lug and short-shift, with fewer gear changes. The trade-off is stronger acceleration and more punishment for an abrupt throttle input.

At 50, with B-rider experience but only seven rides back, separate returning fitness from bike choice. Your Race Tech suspension work also means you’re comparing a tailored bike with a new stock setup.

**My pick for your stated lugging style: a 450 with controllable delivery.** Choose the 350 if reducing fatigue matters more than keeping that effortless low-rpm pull. Before buying, ride a 350 for a full session—not one lap—and compare late-session control and shifting effort, not just acceleration.

Im between 2025 honda 250r and 2024 honda 450r. ... Im 5'9 and about 140 pounds now. ... I've heard that the modern 250s are better for casual riders than back then, meaning that the power is more usable, is that right?

(5'9", ~140 lb, age 36; rode from 14 to 26 as a decent rider; returning; choosing between 2025 CRF250R and 2024 CRF450R)

reply.summary: Pick the 2025 CRF250R for your weight and return to riding. Modern 250 four-strokes generally have more usable power than older generations, but they are still race bikes.
reply.answer:
**I’d pick the 2025 CRF250R for you.** At 140 lb, with solid past experience but roughly ten years off, a 250F gives you plenty to grow back into without the 450’s extra demands.

Yes—**in general, modern 250 four-strokes have broader, cleaner power delivery than older generations**, so you don’t have to ride them flat-out everywhere. I can’t confirm the exact year-to-year power differences for these Hondas here. A 250F still rewards revs and gear changes; it isn’t a mellow trail bike.

The 450’s advantage is effortless pull with fewer shifts. The downside is that a small throttle mistake produces a much bigger response, and managing that drive can wear you out sooner. You don’t need a 450 to avoid outgrowing a 250, especially for casual riding.

At 5'9", neither is automatically too big, but check how comfortably you can balance and stop. At your weight, **budget for suspension setup before power parts**—check rider and free sag to establish whether the springs suit you.

Start back with standing, braking and easy corners, then rebuild jump confidence rather than immediately chasing your old pace. Between these two, the **250R is my straight pick**.

Now I am early 40's ... Right now Im around 240 but plan on lowering that to 200-210. Not very experienced. ... i've had some say get a 450f of sorts, because of my size. What suggestions do you all have for bikes though.

(Early 40s, ~240 lb (aiming for 200-210), not very experienced; previously rode a stripped KLR off-road; considered a 250 EXC for desert)

reply.summary: Your weight calls for the right suspension springs, not automatically a 450. For learning desert and trail riding, my pick is a mellow 350 four-stroke enduro.
reply.answer:
**Don’t buy a 450 just because you weigh 240 lb.** You need suspension suited to your weight; you don’t need race-bike power to move you around.

Assuming desert and trail riding is still the plan:
- **350 four-stroke enduro:** My first pick—something in the KTM 350 EXC-F class. Enough pull to keep as your skills improve, without the abruptness and fatigue of a 450 motocross bike. It still deserves a careful throttle hand.
- **250 four-stroke trail/enduro:** A sensible learning choice. Your weight doesn’t rule it out; you’ll use the gears more in deep sand and on climbs. Choose a trail-oriented model rather than a high-strung motocross bike.
- **250 EXC two-stroke:** Capable, but its stronger power hit and clutch work make it a less forgiving first choice than a mellow four-stroke.

Your stripped KLR experience helps, but a lighter dirt bike can respond much more sharply. **My straight pick: a clean, well-maintained 350 four-stroke enduro, with springs selected for your current riding weight—not your target weight.** Reassess them when you reach 200–210 lb; budget for suspension before exhaust or engine upgrades.
